summary: Give the Stair carpet calculator the effective tread run, the landing depth, the nosing thickness and the extra width and it returns nosing overhang. That makes it useful for a materials order or a planning estimate you want to get roughly right first time. Every field is labelled the way you would say it out loud, so you can usually fill the form from memory and only look up the numbers you genuinely do not know.

sections.title: How does the Stair carpet calculator work?
sections.html:
The Stair carpet calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports nosing overhang in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (with stair nosing overhang? and the nosing shape); then you type in the effective tread run, the landing depth, the nosing thickness and the extra width.

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Stair carpet calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Nosing overhang=(1 ÷ 2) × Y1 ÷ rounded up, ((1 ÷ 1000) × rounded down, (nosing shape) ÷ nosing shape) − 1 ÷ 2 × riser rise
Riser rise=-nosing overhang + nosing thickness + Y2 − the square root of ((nosing overhang ^ 2) + (nosing thickness ^ 2))
Riser rise=(-4 × nosing overhang × rounded up, (nosing thickness × rounded down, (2 × nosing overhang ÷ nosing thickness) ÷ (200 × nosing overhang + nosing thickness)) × rounded up, ((1 ÷ 5) × the absolute value of (5 × nosing shape − 1)) + PI × nosing overhang × rounded up, (nosing thickness × rounded down, (2 × nosing overhang ÷ nosing thickness) ÷ (200 × nosing overhang + nosing thickness)) × rounded up, ((1 ÷ 5) × the absolute value of (5 × nosing shape − 1)) − PI × nosing overhang × rounded up, (nosing thickness × rounded down, (2 × nosing overhang ÷ nosing thickness) ÷ (200 × nosing overhang + nosing thickness)) + 4 × nosing overhang × rounded up, (nosing thickness × rounded down, (2 × nosing overhang ÷ nosing thickness) ÷ (200 × nosing overhang + nosing thickness)) − PI × nosing overhang × rounded up, ((1 ÷ 5) × the absolute value of (5 × nosing shape − 1)) + 2 × nosing overhang × rounded up, ((1 ÷ 5) × the absolute value of (5 × nosing shape − 1)) − 2 × nosing overhang + PI × nosing overhang − 1 ÷ 2 × PI × nosing thickness × rounded up, (nosing thickness × rounded down, (2 × nosing overhang ÷ nosing thickness) ÷ (200 × nosing overhang + nosing thickness)) × rounded up, ((1 ÷ 5) × the absolute value of (5 × nosing shape − 1)) + 2 × nosing thickness × rounded up, (nosing thickness × rounded down, (2 × nosing overhang ÷ nosing thickness) ÷ (200 × nosing overhang + nosing thickness)) × rounded up, ((1 ÷ 5) × the absolute value of (5 × nosing shape − 1)) − 2 × nosing thickness × rounded up, (nosing thickness × rounded down, (2 × nosing overhang ÷ nosing thickness) ÷ (200 × nosing overhang + nosing thickness)) + (1 ÷ 2) × PI × nosing thickness × rounded up, (nosing thickness × rounded down, (2 × nosing overhang ÷ nosing thickness) ÷ (200 × nosing overhang + nosing thickness)) − Y3) ÷ (rounded up, ((1 ÷ 5) × the absolute value of (5 × nosing shape − 1)) − 1)
Y2=(-Y + Y1 + Y3) ÷ (rounded up, (nosing shape − 1 ÷ 10) − 1)
Number of steps=(carpet length (with nosing) + effective tread run − extra length − landing depth) ÷ (effective tread run + Y)
Number of steps=(carpet length + effective tread run − extra length − landing depth) ÷ (effective tread run + riser rise)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Stair carpet calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Quoting a job where areas and quantities drive the price
  • Ordering material and not wanting a second trip
  • Checking a supplier's figure against your own measurements
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the effective tread run, the landing depth and the nosing thickness — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Stair carpet calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns nosing overhang, derived from the effective tread run, the landing depth and the nosing thickness. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Stair carpet calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the effective tread run, the landing depth, the nosing thickness and the extra width, which is 12 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter riser rise in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Riser rise opens in centimeters and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (2 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

faq.q: Is the Stair carpet calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
